blocks.text: 1. overview

blocks.alt: Data points run through K-Means to produce K clusters

blocks.text: Every single algorithm covered so far in this course, from Linear Regression through the entire Classification Algorithms module, shares one thing in common: they all learn from labeled examples, training data where the correct answer, whether a number or a class, is already known. The Clustering Algorithms module marks a genuine turning point. Starting here, there are no labels at all, just raw feature data, and the goal is no longer to predict a known answer but to discover meaningful structure that was never labeled in the first place.

This is unsupervised learning, and K-Means is by far the most widely used, most intuitive algorithm to begin with. Given a collection of unlabeled data points and a chosen number of groups, K-Means finds K cluster centers, called centroids, and assigns every point to whichever centroid it is closest to, iteratively refining both the centroid positions and the point assignments until the arrangement stabilizes. Its simplicity, speed, and genuinely useful results on a huge range of real datasets have made it the default first algorithm to reach for whenever the task is to group similar things together without any predefined categories.
2. Supervised versus Unsupervised Learning

It is worth pausing to make this shift explicit, since it changes how every subsequent topic in this module should be understood. In supervised learning, covered throughout the Regression and Classification modules, every training example comes with a known correct answer, a house price, a class label, and the model is judged directly by how closely its predictions match that known answer on new data.

In unsupervised learning, no such known answer exists anywhere in the data. There is nothing to predict in the traditional sense, only structure to discover: which points naturally belong together, which points stand apart as unusual, which dimensions capture the most meaningful variation. Success in this setting cannot be measured against a ground truth label, since none exists; it has to be measured by how sensible, useful, and internally consistent the discovered structure turns out to be, a genuinely different kind of evaluation problem that resurfaces throughout this entire module.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Despite having no labels, unsupervised learning still relies heavily on the same feature engineering and preprocessing foundations covered earlier in this course, scaling, encoding, and handling missing data all still matter just as much here as they did for Regression and Classification.

blocks.text: 3. The K-Means Algorithm

blocks.alt: Points are assigned to the nearest center, centers are updated, and it repeats until stable

blocks.text: K-Means works through a simple, repeating two-step loop. First, K centroids, one per desired cluster, are placed somewhere in feature space, typically starting at random data points. Every single data point in the dataset is then assigned to whichever of these K centroids it is closest to, using ordinary distance measurement, splitting the data into K groups based purely on proximity.

Second, each centroid is recalculated as the average position, the mean, of every point currently assigned to it, which is exactly why the algorithm is called K-Means. These two steps, assign points to the nearest centroid, then recompute each centroid as the mean of its assigned points, repeat over and over. With each repetition, the centroids shift slightly to better represent their assigned points, and the assignments shift slightly in response to the moved centroids, until eventually neither the assignments nor the centroid positions change meaningfully between rounds, at which point the algorithm has converged.
4. Distance and the Importance of Scaling

blocks.alt: Unscaled features lead to distorted clusters

blocks.text: The point-to-centroid assignment step in K-Means relies on exactly the same kind of distance calculation already covered in depth for KNN back in the Classification module, most commonly plain Euclidean distance. Every point is assigned to whichever centroid it sits closest to in that distance metric, meaning the entire clustering result depends directly on how distance is measured across the feature space.

This makes feature scaling just as critical here as it was for KNN. If one feature spans a much larger numeric range than another, unscaled, that feature will dominate every distance calculation, effectively deciding cluster assignments almost entirely on its own while other, potentially more meaningful features get drowned out. Standardizing every feature to zero mean and unit variance before running K-Means, the same Feature Scaling module technique applied throughout this course, is essential, not optional, for getting clusters that reflect genuine structure in the data rather than an artifact of arbitrary measurement units.
5. Choosing K with the Elbow Method

blocks.alt: Trying many K values reveals an elbow point that chooses the best K

blocks.text: Unlike the classifiers covered in the previous module, K-Means requires the number of clusters, K, to be specified upfront, before the algorithm even begins, and choosing a good value for K is often the single most important decision in the entire clustering process. The most common practical technique is the Elbow Method: run K-Means repeatedly with K set to 1, then 2, then 3, and so on, recording a quantity called inertia for each run.

Inertia always decreases as K increases, since more clusters can only ever fit the data at least as tightly as fewer clusters can, all the way down to zero when K equals the number of data points. The Elbow Method looks for the point on a plot of inertia against K where the rate of improvement drops off sharply, forming a visible elbow shape, since that point represents roughly where adding further clusters stops meaningfully improving the fit relative to the added complexity of tracking more clusters.
6. Inertia: What K-Means Actually Minimizes

blocks.alt: Points in a cluster and their distance to the center together define inertia

blocks.text: Inertia, also called within-cluster sum of squares, WCSS, is the precise mathematical quantity K-Means is designed to minimize. For every single point in the dataset, compute the squared distance between that point and the centroid it has been assigned to, then sum this squared distance across every point in the entire dataset. A lower total inertia means every point sits, on average, closer to its own centroid, indicating tighter, more internally compact clusters.

Every iteration of the K-Means loop, assigning points to their nearest centroid and then recomputing centroids as the mean of their assigned points, provably never increases inertia, and in practice steadily decreases it round after round until convergence. This is precisely why inertia is the natural quantity to track when applying the Elbow Method: it is not an arbitrary external metric but literally the exact objective function K-Means itself is built to optimize.

blocks.text: 7. Assumptions and Limitations

K-Means makes several implicit assumptions that are worth understanding clearly, since violating them can produce genuinely poor clustering results. It implicitly assumes clusters are roughly spherical, or circular in two dimensions, and roughly similar in size, since the mean-based centroid update and simple distance-based assignment naturally favor compact, evenly sized, round groupings. Elongated clusters, clusters of very different densities, or clusters wrapped around each other in non-convex shapes can all confuse K-Means badly, since its underlying geometry simply cannot represent those shapes well.

K-Means is also sensitive to how the initial centroids happen to be placed, since different random starting positions can lead the iterative refinement process to settle into different, sometimes meaningfully worse, final clusterings, an example of the algorithm converging to a local rather than global optimum. Additionally, K-Means forces every single point into some cluster, with no built-in concept of an outlier or noise point that genuinely does not belong anywhere, a limitation that DBSCAN, covered later in this module, was specifically designed to address.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Before trusting a K-Means result, it is worth visually inspecting the clusters if the data allows it, or checking whether the underlying assumption of roughly spherical, similarly sized clusters is plausible for the problem at hand. If it clearly is not, Spectral Clustering or DBSCAN, both covered later in this module, are often better suited.

blocks.text: 8. Smarter Initialization with K-Means++

blocks.alt: Random initialization compares against the smarter start of K-Means++

blocks.text: The sensitivity to initial centroid placement described above has a practical, widely adopted fix called K-Means++. Rather than placing all K initial centroids completely at random, which risks two or more centroids landing close together and effectively wasting a cluster from the very start, K-Means++ places them more deliberately. The very first centroid is still chosen at random from the data points, but every subsequent centroid is chosen with probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest centroid already placed.

This deliberately spreads the initial centroids out across the feature space before the iterative refinement loop even begins, making it far less likely that two centroids start off redundantly close together, and it substantially improves both the speed of convergence and the quality of the final clustering compared to naive random initialization. K-Means++ is the default initialization strategy in scikit-learn precisely because of this reliability improvement, and running K-Means multiple times with different random seeds and keeping the run with the lowest inertia remains a further, complementary safeguard against unlucky initialization.
9. Evaluating Clusters Without Labels

blocks.alt: With no true labels available, a silhouette score evaluates the clusters

blocks.text: Because there are no true labels in unsupervised learning, none of the evaluation metrics used throughout the Regression and Classification modules, accuracy, Log Loss, MSE, apply here at all. A different family of metrics is needed, ones that judge cluster quality using only the structure of the data itself. The Silhouette Score is the most widely used such metric, computed for each individual point by comparing how similar that point is to the other points in its own assigned cluster against how similar it is to the points in the nearest neighboring cluster.

A Silhouette Score near positive 1 indicates a point that fits its cluster well and sits far from any other cluster, a strong sign of good clustering. A score near 0 indicates a point sitting right near the boundary between two clusters, genuinely ambiguous. A score near negative 1 suggests the point may actually have been assigned to the wrong cluster entirely, since it is more similar, on average, to a different cluster than the one it was placed in. Averaging the Silhouette Score across every point in the dataset gives a single overall quality measure, useful both for judging one particular clustering result and for comparing different choices of K directly.

blocks.title: tip
blocks.content: The Silhouette Score and the Elbow Method are complementary, not competing, techniques for choosing K. The Elbow Method looks at the aggregate inertia curve, while the Silhouette Score can reveal problems, like points sitting ambiguously between clusters, that the inertia curve alone would not surface.

blocks.text: 10. Worked Example
The example below fits K-Means with K-Means++ initialization, uses the Elbow Method to compare a few values of K, and computes the Silhouette Score for the final chosen clustering.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

# Two features describing customers: annual spend (thousands), visit frequency per month
X = np.array([
    [2, 1], [3, 2], [2.5, 1.5], [3.2, 2.2],       # low-spend, infrequent group
    [15, 8], [16, 9], [14.5, 7.5], [15.5, 8.5],   # high-spend, frequent group
    [8, 4], [9, 4.5], [7.5, 3.5], [8.5, 4.2],     # mid-spend, moderate group
])

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)

# Elbow Method: compare inertia across a few values of K
for k in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]:
    model = KMeans(n_clusters=k, init='k-means++', n_init=10, random_state=42)
    model.fit(X_scaled)
    print(f"K={k}: inertia={model.inertia_:.2f}")

# Fit the chosen K and evaluate with Silhouette Score
final_model = KMeans(n_clusters=3, init='k-means++', n_init=10, random_state=42)
labels = final_model.fit_predict(X_scaled)
print("Cluster assignments:", labels)
print("Silhouette Score:", silhouette_score(X_scaled, labels))

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: n_init=10 runs the entire K-Means algorithm 10 times with different K-Means++ initializations and automatically keeps the run with the lowest inertia, a practical safeguard against any single unlucky initialization producing a poor result.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: The Clustering Algorithms module begins the unsupervised portion of this course: no labels, only structure to discover.
K-Means alternates between assigning points to their nearest centroid and recomputing centroids as the mean of their assigned points, until convergence.
It minimizes inertia, the sum of squared distances from every point to its assigned centroid, its precise optimization objective.
Distance-based assignment means feature scaling is essential, exactly as it was for KNN in the Classification module.
K must be chosen upfront; the Elbow Method compares inertia across candidate values of K to find a reasonable choice.
K-Means assumes roughly spherical, similarly sized clusters and forces every point into some cluster, with no concept of noise.
K-Means++ initialization spreads initial centroids out deliberately, improving convergence reliability over naive random placement.
The Silhouette Score evaluates clustering quality without labels, comparing within-cluster similarity against nearest-other-cluster similarity.
Next up: Hierarchical Clustering, which builds a full tree of nested clusters instead of requiring K to be chosen in advance.
